pron_note: Also heard as FUL-kruhm, first syllable like *dull*.
means:
The fixed point on which a lever pivots — and, figuratively, the thing on which a whole situation turns.

Size is the point. A fulcrum isn't the biggest or strongest part of the system; it's the *small, still* part that makes enormous force possible. So calling someone the fulcrum of a negotiation says more than "important" — it says the whole weight rests on them, and shift them an inch and the outcome changes. Compare **linchpin** (holds things together, stops collapse) and **crux** (the hard central problem): a fulcrum is about **leverage**, not cohesion or difficulty.
trick_line: **Ful**crum = *full* + *crumb* — a crumb-sized point bearing the full weight.
trick_unpack: The fulcrum is tiny and never moves, yet everything the lever manages to lift depends on it.
sentences: A handful of undecided senators became the **fulcrum** of the entire bill: small in number, decisive in effect.
My gran is the **fulcrum** of that family — take her out and the whole thing tips over.
in_the_wild: The bolt in the middle of a **seesaw** is a fulcrum — which is why shuffling toward the centre kills your leverage and the heavier kid pins you in the air.
etymology: Latin **fulcrum** = *"bedpost, support,"* from **fulcīre**, *"to prop up."* The word has barely changed job in two thousand years: it is still the thing propping everything else up.
one_line: The pivot point a lever turns on; the decisive thing.
